# Scotland EPC

It is part of Scottish Energy Services (https://www.scottishenergyservices.co.uk/), 272 Bath Street, Glasgow G2 4JR. EPCs are produced by accredited domestic energy assessors and lodged on the Scottish EPC Register, normally within 24 hours of the visit.

- Turnaround: EPC normally lodged and emailed within 24 hours of the visit
- Scottish EPC rules: current EPCs valid 10 years; rating must appear in adverts; EPC must be fixed in the property (often meter cupboard or by the boiler); £500 penalty charge for homes
- EPC reform: from 30 April 2028 new-style Scottish EPCs with Heat Retention, Heating System and Energy Cost ratings, valid five years; transition to 30 April 2029
- Legionella: Repairing Standard guidance requires private landlords to assess legionella risk before first let and review at intervals of no more than two years; no legionella certificate exists

### Two checks every Scottish let needs

An EPC before the property is advertised, and a legionella risk assessment before the tenant moves in. We do both, separately or together.

#### Domestic EPC

An Energy Performance Certificate rates a home from A to G and lists the improvements that would raise it. You need one before a home is marketed for sale or let, and it currently lasts 10 years.

- Survey by an accredited domestic energy assessor
 
- Lodged on the Scottish EPC Register, so buyers, tenants and agents can find it
 
- Recommendations report with typical costs and savings
 
- Advice on where to fix it in the property, as Scottish rules require
 
 from £70 flats, from £85 houses, plus VATAbout domestic EPCs

#### Legionella risk assessment

Scottish landlords must have the hot and cold water system assessed before a property is first let, then reviewed at least every two years.

- Temperatures measured at the taps, cylinder and tank
 
- Tank, shower, dead legs and little-used outlets checked
 
- Written assessment with a clear, short action list
 
- Plain-English guidance you can hand to tenants
 
 from £65 per property, plus VATAbout legionella assessments

#### Both in one visit for £120 + VAT

An EPC and a legionella risk assessment at the same appointment, so your tenant or agent only has to give access once.
 Book both

### See what we check in your home

The same visit seen two ways. Switch between the EPC survey and the legionella assessment, then tap a number to see what the assessor looks at and why it matters.

- 
We measure the depth of loft insulation, or note a room in the roof. Topping a loft up to 270mm is one of the cheapest ways to move up a band.
- 
Wall type and thickness tell us whether walls are solid stone, cavity or timber frame, and whether they have been insulated. Glasgow and Edinburgh sandstone often has no insulation at all.
- 
We record the glazing type and roughly when it was fitted, and how much of each wall is glass.
- 
The make and model let us look up the boiler's tested efficiency. An older non-condensing boiler can cost a home a whole band.
- 
Room thermostat, programmer and radiator valves all count. Missing controls are a quick win in the recommendations.
- 
If there is a cylinder, we check its insulation jacket or foam and whether it has a thermostat.
- 
We count fixed light fittings and how many are low-energy. LEDs throughout are worth having.
- 
Solar PV, solar water heating and heat pumps are recorded with their size. Renewables lift both the rating and the potential.
- 
In Scotland the EPC must be fixed somewhere in the property, often in the meter cupboard or beside the boiler. We remind you where it should go.
- 
Loft tanks should have a tight lid, be insulated and stay below 20°C. We look for debris, rust and signs the water sits still.
- 
Stored hot water should reach 60°C. We check the thermostat setting and record the temperature at the nearest tap.
- 
With a combi there is no stored hot water, which lowers the risk. We record the system type and how hot water reaches each outlet.
- 
Showers create the fine spray that carries legionella. We check the head and hose for scale and whether the shower is used.
- 
We run hot and cold taps and measure the temperature. Hot should reach 50°C within a minute and cold should be below 20°C within two minutes.
- 
Taps in spare rooms or empty flats let water stagnate. We note them so they can be flushed weekly when the property is empty.
- 
Pipework that leads to an outlet that was taken out holds still water. Redundant pipes and dead legs should be removed.
- 
Outside taps and hoses can hold warm stagnant water in summer. We note them and give simple flushing advice.

### Why water temperature matters

Legionella bacteria live naturally in water. They become a risk when water sits at the wrong temperature and is then breathed in as fine spray, usually from a shower. Keeping hot water hot and cold water cold is the main control in a home.
 
Drag the slider or pick a typical reading to see what each temperature means. These are the same readings we take on a visit.

- Hot water stored at 60°C or above
 
- Hot water at least 50°C at the tap within a minute
 
- Cold water below 20°C within two minutes
 
 What a legionella risk assessment covers

Temperature bands from HSE guidance on legionella in hot and cold water systems.

### EPCs are changing in 2028

From 30 April 2028 Scotland moves to a new style of EPC with three headline ratings instead of one, and new certificates will last five years instead of ten.
 
An EPC you get now stays valid for its full 10 years for most purposes, and can still be used to sell or let during a one-year transition. If you are letting or selling in the next 18 months, there is no reason to wait.
 Read the 2028 guide

- 
TodayIn force

#### Current EPCs

RdSAP survey, one A to G energy efficiency rating, valid for 10 years. Needed before you market a home for sale or let.
- 
31 October 2026In force

#### Register fee rise

The fee for lodging an EPC on the Scottish EPC Register went up to fund the new digital register and methodology.
- 
30 April 2028Confirmed

#### New-style EPCs only

Three headline ratings: Heat Retention, Heating System and Energy Cost. New EPCs are valid for five years and come with a property report.
- 
30 April 2028 to 30 April 2029Confirmed

#### One-year transition

An old-style EPC under 10 years old can still be used to sell or let. If the property is sold or let again in that year, a new-style EPC is needed.
- 
From 30 April 2029Confirmed

#### Old EPCs retired

Only new-style EPCs can be used for a sale or a new let.
- 
ProposedProposed

#### Minimum standard for private lets

Draft plans would require private rented homes to reach Heat Retention Rating band C, first at a change of tenancy and later for all lets. The timetable has not been confirmed.

### Questions we get asked

How much does an EPC cost?
Our domestic EPCs start from £70 for a flat, £75 for a maisonette, £80 for a bungalow and £85 for a house. A legionella risk assessment starts from £65, and both together are £120. All prices are plus VAT, and a £20 travel supplement applies outside Glasgow (G) and Edinburgh (EH) postcodes.
 
How long does an EPC last in Scotland?
A current Scottish EPC is valid for 10 years. From 30 April 2028 new-style EPCs will be valid for five years. Existing EPCs can still be used during a one-year transition to 30 April 2029, with some limits.
 
Do I need an EPC to rent out a property in Scotland?
Yes. You need a valid EPC before the property is advertised, the rating must appear in adverts, and you must give a copy to the tenant. In Scotland the EPC must also be fixed somewhere in the property, such as the meter cupboard or beside the boiler. Councils can issue a £500 penalty for a home without one.
 
Do Scottish landlords need a legionella risk assessment?
Yes. The Scottish Government's Repairing Standard guidance says landlords must have the water system assessed for legionella before a property is first let, and review the assessment at intervals of no more than two years.
 
Is there such a thing as a legionella certificate?
No. The law asks for a risk assessment, not a certificate or a water test. You get a written assessment that records what was checked, the temperatures found and any actions needed. Water sampling is not normally needed in a home.
 
Do I need to be at the property?
No, but someone needs to let us in. Many landlords arrange access through their tenant or letting agent. We need to see every room, the boiler, the loft hatch if there is one and the hot water cylinder.

More questions and answers

# Domestic EPC Scotland | From £70 | Lodged Within 24 Hours | Scotland EPC
URL: https://scotlandepc.com/domestic-epc/

- Home
- Domestic EPC

## Domestic EPCs in Scotland

An Energy Performance Certificate shows how efficient a home is and what would improve it. Here is what it covers, when Scottish law requires one, and what happens when we visit.
Updated 18 November 2026

### What an EPC shows

A domestic EPC rates a home's energy efficiency on a scale from A, the most efficient, to G, the least. The band comes from a score between 1 and 100, worked out from the size of the home, how it is built and insulated, how it is heated and how hot water is provided. The certificate also gives an environmental impact rating based on carbon dioxide emissions, estimated energy costs and a potential rating if the recommended improvements were made.
EPC energy efficiency bands and SAP points
Band | SAP points | What it usually means | 
A | 92–100 | Very efficient. Usually new homes with heat pumps or solar. | 
B | 81–91 | Typical of homes built since about 2010. | 
C | 69–80 | Good. A well-insulated older home with an efficient boiler. | 
D | 55–68 | The most common band for Scottish homes. | 
E | 39–54 | Poor insulation or older heating. | 
F | 21–38 | Often electric heating with little insulation. | 
G | 1–20 | Very inefficient and expensive to heat. | 

Every Scottish EPC comes with a recommendations report. It lists improvements such as loft or wall insulation, a new boiler or heating controls, with an indication of cost and how much each could move the rating. You are not obliged to carry any of them out.

### When you need an EPC in Scotland

- Letting a home. You need a valid EPC before the property is advertised, and you must make it available to anyone interested in renting it.
 
- Selling a home. Most sales need a Home Report, which includes the EPC. If a sale is exempt from the Home Report, you still need an EPC before marketing.
 
- New homes and conversions. A new building needs an EPC when it is completed.

Three rules catch people out in Scotland:

- The EPC rating must appear in any advert for the sale or let, including online listings.
 
- The EPC must be fixed somewhere in the property. The meter cupboard or beside the boiler is the usual place.
 
- Your council can issue a penalty charge of £500 if a home is marketed without a valid EPC.

You can check whether a home already has a valid EPC by searching the address on the Scottish EPC Register. If yours is less than 10 years old and nothing major has changed, you may not need a new one, although a new survey can show improvements the old one missed.

### How long an EPC lasts

A current Scottish EPC is valid for 10 years. From 30 April 2028 the Scottish Government is introducing new-style EPCs with three headline ratings, valid for five years. There is a one-year transition for existing certificates. Our guide to the 2028 changes sets out the dates.

### What happens on the survey

An accredited domestic energy assessor visits and records the details the rating is calculated from. We need to see every room, the boiler and heating controls, the hot water cylinder if there is one, and the loft if it can be reached safely. Most visits take under an hour.

- 
We measure the depth of loft insulation, or note a room in the roof. Topping a loft up to 270mm is one of the cheapest ways to move up a band.
- 
Wall type and thickness tell us whether walls are solid stone, cavity or timber frame, and whether they have been insulated. Glasgow and Edinburgh sandstone often has no insulation at all.
- 
We record the glazing type and roughly when it was fitted, and how much of each wall is glass.
- 
The make and model let us look up the boiler's tested efficiency. An older non-condensing boiler can cost a home a whole band.
- 
Room thermostat, programmer and radiator valves all count. Missing controls are a quick win in the recommendations.
- 
If there is a cylinder, we check its insulation jacket or foam and whether it has a thermostat.
- 
We count fixed light fittings and how many are low-energy. LEDs throughout are worth having.
- 
Solar PV, solar water heating and heat pumps are recorded with their size. Renewables lift both the rating and the potential.
- 
In Scotland the EPC must be fixed somewhere in the property, often in the meter cupboard or beside the boiler. We remind you where it should go.
- 
Loft tanks should have a tight lid, be insulated and stay below 20°C. We look for debris, rust and signs the water sits still.
- 
Stored hot water should reach 60°C. We check the thermostat setting and record the temperature at the nearest tap.
- 
With a combi there is no stored hot water, which lowers the risk. We record the system type and how hot water reaches each outlet.
- 
Showers create the fine spray that carries legionella. We check the head and hose for scale and whether the shower is used.
- 
We run hot and cold taps and measure the temperature. Hot should reach 50°C within a minute and cold should be below 20°C within two minutes.
- 
Taps in spare rooms or empty flats let water stagnate. We note them so they can be flushed weekly when the property is empty.
- 
Pipework that leads to an outlet that was taken out holds still water. Redundant pipes and dead legs should be removed.
- 
Outside taps and hoses can hold warm stagnant water in summer. We note them and give simple flushing advice.

#### Things that help on the day

- Access to the loft hatch and the boiler cupboard.
 
- Paperwork for anything we cannot see: cavity wall insulation guarantees, receipts or certificates for loft or wall insulation, window installation dates, solar panel or heat pump certificates.
 
- A note of any extensions or rooms in the roof, with roughly when they were built.

Evidence matters. Without it the assessor has to use default assumptions for the age of the home, which can understate the rating.

### After the visit

We produce the EPC and lodge it on the Scottish EPC Register, normally within 24 hours of the visit. You get the certificate and recommendations report by email, ready to send to your agent or add to your listing.

### Improving your rating

The quickest wins in a Scottish home are usually loft insulation, filling empty cavity walls, upgrading an old boiler, adding heating controls and low-energy lighting. Older sandstone tenements are harder to improve because the walls are solid and many sit in conservation areas. Try our EPC rating estimator to see which changes would make the biggest difference to a home like yours.

### Domestic EPC questions

Who can produce an EPC in Scotland?
Only an assessor who belongs to an approved organisation can produce and lodge a Scottish EPC. Every EPC we issue is produced by an accredited domestic energy assessor and lodged on the Scottish EPC Register.

Do I need a new EPC for each new tenant?
No. One valid EPC covers every new let during its 10-year life. You need a new one when it expires before you market the property again.

Can tenants be in the property during the survey?
Yes. Let them know we will need to see every room and the boiler, and lift the loft hatch if there is one.

Does a listed building need an EPC?
Yes. Unlike in England and Wales, listed and historic buildings in Scotland have no general exemption, so they need an EPC when sold or let like any other home. Many improvements that raise the rating need consent in listed buildings and conservation areas, so check with your council before making changes.

Written by the Scotland EPC team at Scottish Energy Services, Glasgow. Last checked against Scottish Government and HSE guidance on 18 November 2026. This page is general guidance, not legal advice.

# Legionella Risk Assessment for Landlords in Scotland | From £65 | Scotland EPC
URL: https://scotlandepc.com/legionella-risk-assessment/

- Home
- Legionella risk assessment

## Legionella risk assessments for Scottish landlords

Every private let in Scotland needs its water system assessed for legionella before the first tenancy, and reviewed at least every two years. We do it in one short visit and send you a clear written assessment.
Updated 18 November 2026

### What the law requires in Scotland

Landlords have a duty under health and safety law to assess and control the risk of tenants being exposed to legionella. In Scotland this is spelled out in the Scottish Government's statutory guidance on the Repairing Standard, which private landlords must have regard to. It says:

- all water systems must be assessed for legionella risk before the property is first let;
 
- the risk assessment should be reviewed at intervals of no more than two years, and a new one carried out if anything significant has changed;
 
- to help control the risk, landlords should flush the system before letting if this has not been done in the previous two years, make sure cold water tanks have a tight-fitting lid, set stored hot water to at least 60°C, and remove redundant pipework and dead ends.

The same guidance applies to short-term lets, which must also meet the Repairing Standard. The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) enforces the underlying duty.

There is no such thing as a legionella certificate. The law asks for a risk assessment. Water sampling or laboratory testing is not normally needed in a home, and a test on its own does not show the risk is being managed.

### Can I do it myself?

You can, if you are competent to do so. HSE guidance accepts that many landlords of simple domestic systems assess the risk themselves. Many landlords and letting agents prefer an independent assessment because it is quick, it measures temperatures properly, and it gives them a record they can show a tenant, an agent or the First-tier Tribunal if the Repairing Standard is ever questioned.

### What we check

Switch to the water view below and tap through the points we look at on a typical visit.

- 
We measure the depth of loft insulation, or note a room in the roof. Topping a loft up to 270mm is one of the cheapest ways to move up a band.
- 
Wall type and thickness tell us whether walls are solid stone, cavity or timber frame, and whether they have been insulated. Glasgow and Edinburgh sandstone often has no insulation at all.
- 
We record the glazing type and roughly when it was fitted, and how much of each wall is glass.
- 
The make and model let us look up the boiler's tested efficiency. An older non-condensing boiler can cost a home a whole band.
- 
Room thermostat, programmer and radiator valves all count. Missing controls are a quick win in the recommendations.
- 
If there is a cylinder, we check its insulation jacket or foam and whether it has a thermostat.
- 
We count fixed light fittings and how many are low-energy. LEDs throughout are worth having.
- 
Solar PV, solar water heating and heat pumps are recorded with their size. Renewables lift both the rating and the potential.
- 
In Scotland the EPC must be fixed somewhere in the property, often in the meter cupboard or beside the boiler. We remind you where it should go.
- 
Loft tanks should have a tight lid, be insulated and stay below 20°C. We look for debris, rust and signs the water sits still.
- 
Stored hot water should reach 60°C. We check the thermostat setting and record the temperature at the nearest tap.
- 
With a combi there is no stored hot water, which lowers the risk. We record the system type and how hot water reaches each outlet.
- 
Showers create the fine spray that carries legionella. We check the head and hose for scale and whether the shower is used.
- 
We run hot and cold taps and measure the temperature. Hot should reach 50°C within a minute and cold should be below 20°C within two minutes.
-

- 
Pipework that leads to an outlet that was taken out holds still water. Redundant pipes and dead legs should be removed.
- 
Outside taps and hoses can hold warm stagnant water in summer. We note them and give simple flushing advice.

On every visit we:

- identify the type of hot and cold water system, from a simple combi boiler to a cylinder fed by a loft tank;
 
- measure water temperatures at the taps, the cylinder and any cold water tank;
 
- inspect tanks for lids, insulation, debris and rust;
 
- look for dead legs, redundant pipework and outlets that are rarely used;
 
- check showers, mixer valves and outside taps;
 
- note anything about the tenants or the use of the property that raises the risk, such as long empty periods.

### The temperatures that matter

Temperature is the main control in a home. Legionella bacteria multiply in water between 20°C and 45°C, are dormant below 20°C and do not survive above 60°C. Try the slider to see what each reading means.

Temperature bands from HSE guidance on legionella in hot and cold water systems.

### What you get

- A written legionella risk assessment for the property, with the date and the assessor's name.
 
- The temperatures we recorded and where.
 
- An overall risk level and a short list of actions, if any are needed, in order of priority.
 
- A plain-English sheet for your tenants about keeping the water system safe.
 
- A reminder of when the assessment should be reviewed.

Most homes with a combi boiler and no stored water come out as low risk with few or no actions. Homes with loft tanks, hot water cylinders, long pipe runs or periods standing empty are where we most often find something to fix.

### Keeping the risk low between assessments

- Run taps and showers that are not used often for a couple of minutes once a week, especially in empty properties.
 
- Flush the system before a new tenant moves in if the property has stood empty.
 
- Clean and descale shower heads regularly.
 
- Keep the cylinder thermostat at 60°C and ask tenants not to turn it down.
 
- Have redundant pipework removed when other plumbing work is being done.

### Price

A legionella risk assessment starts from £65 + VAT per property in Glasgow (G) and Edinburgh (EH) postcodes, or £120 + VAT with an EPC at the same visit. Larger shared systems, such as in HMOs or blocks with communal tanks, are quoted individually. Get a price.

### Legionella questions

How often does a legionella risk assessment need to be done in Scotland?
Before a property is first let, then reviewed at intervals of no more than two years under the Repairing Standard guidance. Review it sooner if the water system changes, for example a new boiler or cylinder, or if the property has stood empty.

Is a property with a combi boiler still covered?
Yes. A combi boiler with no stored water is usually low risk, but the duty to assess still applies. The assessment confirms the system type, checks temperatures and looks at showers and little-used outlets.

Do HMOs need a legionella risk assessment?
Yes. HMOs often have larger or shared systems with storage tanks, so the assessment takes longer. Tell us about the property and we will quote.

What is Legionnaires' disease?
A potentially fatal form of pneumonia caused by breathing in tiny water droplets containing legionella bacteria. People over 45, smokers and those with weakened immune systems are at higher risk. It is not caught by drinking water.

Written by the Scotland EPC team at Scottish Energy Services, Glasgow. Last checked against Scottish Government and HSE guidance on 18 November 2026. This page is general guidance, not legal advice.

# EPC Rating Estimator for Scottish Homes | Free | Scotland EPC
URL: https://scotlandepc.com/epc-rating-estimator/

- Home
- EPC rating estimator

## EPC rating estimator

Answer a few questions about your home to get a rough EPC band, then tick improvements to see how far each could move it. Free, instant, and nothing is stored.

#### Try an improvement

A rough guide based on typical Scottish homes, not an EPC. A real rating needs a survey by an accredited assessor.

### How the estimate works

The estimator starts from a typical rating for a Scottish home of that age, then adjusts it for the type of home, the heating, insulation, windows and solar panels. The figures are based on how these features usually affect a domestic EPC. They are deliberately simple.

This is a rough guide, not an EPC. A real rating is calculated by an accredited assessor from measurements of the home, its exact heating system and evidence of insulation, and is the only rating you can use to sell or let. Results can differ by a band or more.

### What moves a rating most

#### Heating

The main heating system has the biggest single effect. Replacing an old non-condensing gas boiler or direct electric heating usually moves a home up at least one band.

#### Walls

Filling empty cavity walls is cheap and effective. Solid sandstone and brick walls can be insulated internally or externally, but the work is more involved, especially in tenements and conservation areas.

#### Loft

Topping loft insulation up to 270mm is one of the cheapest improvements for houses and top-floor flats with their own loft.

#### Renewables

Solar PV panels and heat pumps lift both the current and potential ratings. They are recorded on the EPC with their size.

### EPC bands explained

EPC energy efficiency bands and SAP points
Band | SAP points | What it usually means | 
A | 92–100 | Very efficient. Usually new homes with heat pumps or solar. | 
B | 81–91 | Typical of homes built since about 2010. | 
C | 69–80 | Good. A well-insulated older home with an efficient boiler. | 
D | 55–68 | The most common band for Scottish homes. | 
E | 39–54 | Poor insulation or older heating. | 
F | 21–38 | Often electric heating with little insulation. | 
G | 1–20 | Very inefficient and expensive to heat. | 

The Scottish Government has proposed that private rented homes should reach Heat Retention Rating band C under the new-style EPC, which measures insulation rather than running costs. It is not the same scale as today's rating. Our 2028 guide explains the difference.

A domestic EPC costs from £70 for a flat and from £85 for a house, plus VAT, and the recommendations report tells you exactly which improvements apply to your home. Get a price or call 07483 881889.

# EPC Changes in Scotland 2028: New Ratings & 5-Year Validity | Scotland EPC
URL: https://scotlandepc.com/epc-changes-2028/

- Home
- EPC changes 2028

## EPC changes in Scotland from 2028

Scotland is replacing the EPC with a new certificate that has three headline ratings and lasts five years. The start date has moved to 30 April 2028. Here is what changes, what stays the same, and what to do now.
Updated 18 November 2026

### The short version

- Today's EPCs, with one A to G rating and 10-year validity, carry on until 30 April 2028.
 
- From 30 April 2028, new EPCs will have three headline ratings: Heat Retention, Heating System and Energy Cost.
 
- New-style EPCs will be valid for five years, not ten, and come with a property report instead of a recommendations report.
 
- An old-style EPC can still be used to sell or let during a one-year transition to 30 April 2029.
 
- A minimum standard for private lets, based on the new Heat Retention Rating, has been proposed but not yet confirmed.

### Key dates

- 
TodayIn force

#### Current EPCs

RdSAP survey, one A to G energy efficiency rating, valid for 10 years. Needed before you market a home for sale or let.
- 
31 October 2026In force

#### Register fee rise

The fee for lodging an EPC on the Scottish EPC Register went up to fund the new digital register and methodology.
- 
30 April 2028Confirmed

#### New-style EPCs only

Three headline ratings: Heat Retention, Heating System and Energy Cost. New EPCs are valid for five years and come with a property report.
- 
30 April 2028 to 30 April 2029Confirmed

#### One-year transition

An old-style EPC under 10 years old can still be used to sell or let. If the property is sold or let again in that year, a new-style EPC is needed.
- 
From 30 April 2029Confirmed

#### Old EPCs retired

Only new-style EPCs can be used for a sale or a new let.
- 
ProposedProposed

#### Minimum standard for private lets

Draft plans would require private rented homes to reach Heat Retention Rating band C, first at a change of tenancy and later for all lets. The timetable has not been confirmed.

### Why the date moved

The reform was due on 31 October 2026. In August 2026 the Scottish Government laid amending regulations moving the start to 30 April 2028. The new EPCs depend on the UK Government's Home Energy Model, which replaces the current SAP and RdSAP calculation method, and on a new digital EPC Register. Both were delayed across the UK, so Scotland aligned its timetable. The policy itself has not changed.

### The three new ratings

#### Heat Retention Rating

How well the building holds on to heat, from A to G, based on the fabric: walls, roof, floor, windows and draughts. It ignores the heating system.

#### Heating System Rating

How good the main heating system is, taking account of its efficiency, emissions and running costs.

#### Energy Cost Rating

The modelled cost of running the home, closest to today's headline rating, which is also cost based.

The new certificate will also show carbon dioxide emissions. Splitting the rating means a well-insulated home with old heating, or a poorly insulated home with a heat pump, will no longer be hidden behind one blended number.

### Five-year validity

New-style EPCs will be valid for five years. If you let a property, plan for a new EPC roughly twice as often as now. Old-style EPCs issued before 30 April 2028 keep their 10-year validity, but after 30 April 2029 only a new-style EPC can be used for a sale or a new let.

### The transition, step by step

- Before 30 April 2028. Nothing changes. Assessors issue current-style EPCs, valid for 10 years.
 
- From 30 April 2028. Any new EPC must be new style. You can still use a valid old-style EPC for a sale or let.
 
- 30 April 2028 to 30 April 2029. If a property marketed on an old-style EPC is sold or let again within this year, a new-style EPC and property report will be needed.
 
- From 30 April 2029. Only new-style EPCs can be used for sales and new lets.

### The proposed standard for private lets

The Scottish Government has consulted on draft regulations that would require private rented homes to reach Heat Retention Rating band C. The consultation proposed applying it first to new tenancies from 2028 and to all private lets by 2033, with a cost cap and exemptions. Because the rating cannot be produced until new-style EPCs exist, the timetable is likely to move with the EPC reform and has not been confirmed.

The Scottish Government has said it intends Heat Retention band C to be broadly equivalent to today's EPC band C, but it measures something different. A home that is C today because of a cheap-to-run heating system could fall short on heat retention, and the reverse.

### What to do now

#### If you are letting in the next 18 months

Get a current-style EPC as normal. It stays valid for 10 years and can be used through the transition. Read the recommendations report: insulation work you do now will count towards Heat Retention later.

#### If you are selling

Your Home Report will include an EPC as now. Buyers will increasingly look at insulation, so evidence of loft, wall and window upgrades is worth keeping.

#### If you own an older home

Fabric improvements such as loft insulation, cavity wall insulation, draught-proofing and better glazing will matter most under the Heat Retention Rating. Our estimator gives a feel for what changes make a difference.

### Sources

- Scottish Government: Energy Performance Certificate reform updates
 
- Scottish Parliament Economy, Tourism and Energy Committee report on the Energy Performance of Buildings (Scotland) Amendment Regulations 2026
 
- Scottish Government: consultation on draft minimum energy efficiency regulations for the private rented sector

Written by the Scotland EPC team at Scottish Energy Services, Glasgow. Last checked against Scottish Government and HSE guidance on 18 November 2026. This page is general guidance, not legal advice.

# EPC & Legionella Questions Answered | Scotland EPC
URL: https://scotlandepc.com/faq/

- Home
- Questions and answers

## Questions and answers

Straight answers to the questions landlords, agents, sellers and homeowners ask us most.

### Prices and booking

How much does an EPC cost?
From £70 for a flat, £75 for a maisonette, £80 for a bungalow and £85 for a house in Glasgow (G) and Edinburgh (EH) postcodes, plus VAT. Elsewhere in the Central Belt we add £20 for travel.

How much is a legionella risk assessment?
From £65 per property, or £120 together with an EPC at the same visit, plus VAT. HMOs and properties with shared tanks are quoted individually.

Do your prices include VAT?
No. All our prices are shown excluding VAT, which is added at the current rate.

How soon can you come out?
Tell us your deadline when you get in touch. We reply to quote requests the same working day where we can and will offer the earliest time that suits you or your tenant.

How quickly will I get the EPC?
We normally lodge the EPC on the Scottish EPC Register and email it to you within 24 hours of the visit.

Can you book several properties at once?
Yes. List the addresses in the notes on the quote form or call 07483 881889, and we will arrange them in a sensible order.

### About EPCs

How long does an EPC last in Scotland?
Ten years for current EPCs. From 30 April 2028, new-style EPCs will be valid for five years. Existing EPCs can still be used during a one-year transition to 30 April 2029.

What is changing with EPCs in 2028?
New-style EPCs will show three headline ratings, for heat retention, the heating system and energy cost, instead of one. They will be valid for five years and come with a property report. See our 2028 guide.

Do I need an EPC to sell my home in Scotland?
Yes. For most sales the EPC is part of the Home Report. If your sale is exempt from the Home Report, you still need an EPC before marketing the home.

Where does the EPC have to be displayed?
In Scotland the EPC must be fixed somewhere in the property, usually in the meter cupboard or next to the boiler. The rating must also appear in adverts for a sale or let.

What happens if I market a property without an EPC?
The council can issue a penalty charge notice of £500 for a home, and buyers and tenants are entitled to see one before they commit.

How can I check if a property already has an EPC?
Search the address on the Scottish EPC Register. It shows the rating, the date and when it expires.

Can I improve my rating before the survey?
Yes. Fit low-energy bulbs, make sure the heating controls are working, and gather paperwork for insulation, windows, the boiler and any solar panels. Evidence lets the assessor record what is really there instead of using defaults for the age of the home.

### About legionella

Do landlords in Scotland need a legionella risk assessment?
Yes. The Repairing Standard guidance says the water system must be assessed before the property is first let and the assessment reviewed at intervals of no more than two years.

Is there a legionella certificate?
No. The requirement is a risk assessment. Water testing is not normally needed in a home.

What temperatures should my water be?
Stored hot water at 60°C, hot water at the taps at least 50°C within a minute, and cold water below 20°C within two minutes. Legionella can multiply between 20°C and 45°C.

Do short-term lets need one?
Yes. Short-term lets must meet the Repairing Standard, which includes the duty to assess legionella risk.

### On the day

Do I need to be there?
No, as long as someone can let us in. Tenants and letting agents often arrange access.

What do you need to see?
Every room, the boiler and heating controls, the hot water cylinder if there is one, the loft hatch if it can be reached safely, and the taps and showers if you have booked a legionella assessment.

How long does the visit take?
Most visits take under an hour. Larger houses, and EPC and legionella together, take a little longer.

## EPC Glasgow

Domestic EPCs across every Glasgow postcode, from city-centre flats to Southside tenements and suburban houses. No travel charge in G postcodes, and your EPC normally lodged within 24 hours.

### Homes in Glasgow

Glasgow's housing is dominated by flats. Red and blond sandstone tenements fill the West End, Partick, Dennistoun, Shawlands and Strathbungo, alongside interwar and post-war homes in the outer neighbourhoods and newer flats along the Clyde. Each brings its own EPC issues:

- Sandstone tenements have thick solid walls with no cavity to fill, so the rating depends heavily on the heating, the windows and whether the flat is on a middle floor, the top floor or the ground floor.

- Top-floor flats lose heat through the roof. If there is a loft above, insulation there can make a real difference, but it is often shared, so evidence of any work matters.

- Flats with electric heating , common in 1960s and 1970s blocks and some conversions, often rate E or lower. High heat retention storage heaters are the usual recommendation.

- Newer flats and houses built since around 2010 usually rate B or C.

We are based at 272 Bath Street in the city centre, so most Glasgow appointments are close by. We regularly work for landlords and letting agents in the West End, Southside, Merchant City and Finnieston, where the EPC and the legionella risk assessment are often booked together.

## EPC Edinburgh

Domestic EPCs across Edinburgh, from New Town and Marchmont flats to Leith, Portobello and the suburbs. No travel charge in EH postcodes.

### Homes in Edinburgh

Much of Edinburgh's housing is older and protected, which shapes both the rating and what can be done about it:

- Georgian and Victorian tenements in the New Town, Stockbridge, Marchmont and Bruntsfield have solid stone walls, large sash windows and high ceilings. They often rate D or E.

- Listed buildings and conservation areas cover large parts of the city. In Scotland they still need an EPC when sold or let, but changes such as replacement windows or external insulation need consent, so secondary glazing and draught-proofing are often the practical options.

- Leith and the waterfront mix older tenements with modern flats that usually rate B or C.

- Suburban houses in areas like Corstorphine, Liberton and the south of the city are typically interwar or post-war, where loft and cavity insulation are the main recommendations.

Edinburgh has a large private rented sector, student lets and HMOs. Short-term let hosts must meet the Repairing Standard too, which includes the duty to assess legionella risk. We can do the EPC and the legionella risk assessment in one visit for £120 + VAT.

## EPC Bearsden

Domestic EPCs for Bearsden homes, from sandstone villas to interwar bungalows and family houses. No travel charge in G61 or neighbouring Milngavie (G62).

### Homes in Bearsden

Bearsden is mostly houses rather than flats, and many are larger or older than average:

- Victorian and Edwardian villas with solid stone walls, bay windows and rooms in the roof. Extensions built at different times are common, so the assessor records each part separately.

- Interwar bungalows and semis , often with cavity walls. Filled cavities and good loft insulation usually lift these to C or D.

- Post-war and newer detached houses , where the boiler and heating controls make the biggest difference.

Larger homes with several extensions take a little longer to survey. Having the dates of extensions and any insulation paperwork to hand helps the rating reflect the work you have done.

## EPC Bishopbriggs

Domestic EPCs for Bishopbriggs, Torrance and Kirkintilloch, with no travel charge in G64 and G66 postcodes.

### Homes in Bishopbriggs

Bishopbriggs grew quickly from the 1930s onwards, so most homes are semis, bungalows and terraces from the middle of the twentieth century, with newer estates on the edges:

- 1930s to 1970s semis and bungalows usually have cavity walls. Whether the cavity has been filled, and how thick the loft insulation is, decide a lot of the rating.

- Newer estates built since the 1990s are often timber frame with insulation built in, and usually rate C or better.

- Flats around the town centre and Kirkintilloch, where the heating system is the main factor.

If you have had cavity wall insulation installed, a guarantee from the installer is the best evidence, because the assessor cannot always confirm it by looking at the outside of the wall.

# Legionella Risk Assessment Glasgow | From £65 | Scotland EPC
URL: https://scotlandepc.com/legionella-risk-assessment-glasgow/

- Home
- Areas
- Legionella Glasgow

## Legionella risk assessment Glasgow

Legionella risk assessments for rented flats and houses across every Glasgow postcode. From £65 per property, or £120 with an EPC at the same visit, plus VAT.

### Glasgow water systems

Most Glasgow rented flats have one of two systems, and the risk is quite different:

- Combi boilers heat water on demand with nothing stored, so they are usually low risk. We still check outlet temperatures, showers and any little-used taps.

- Hot water cylinders , often with an electric immersion heater in older tenements and 1960s to 1970s flats. Here we check the cylinder reaches 60°C and the hot water at the taps reaches 50°C. Top-floor flats sometimes have a cold water tank in the loft above.

Houses in the suburbs are more likely to have a loft tank and cylinder, which is where we most often find a missing lid, debris or warm cold water.

### Empty flats and student lets

Water that sits still is the biggest risk. Flats that stand empty between tenancies, and student lets over the summer, should have every outlet flushed before the next tenant moves in. We include this in the action list if it applies.

### What we check

We identify the water system, measure temperatures at the taps, cylinder and any tank, inspect tanks for lids and debris, and look for showers, dead legs and little-used outlets. You get a written assessment with the temperatures recorded, an overall risk level and a short list of actions. More about legionella risk assessments.

Temperature bands from HSE guidance on legionella in hot and cold water systems.

### The rules in Scotland

The Repairing Standard guidance says a private landlord must have the water system assessed for legionella before the property is first let, and review it at intervals of no more than two years. There is no legionella certificate and water testing is not normally needed.

### Questions

How much is a legionella risk assessment in Glasgow?
From £65 per property in any G postcode, or £120 with an EPC at the same visit, plus VAT.
How long does it take?
Usually well under an hour for a flat, a little longer for a house with a loft tank.

### Prices

Starting prices, excluding VAT

Flat EPC: from £70 | 
 
Maisonette EPC: from £75 | 
 
Bungalow EPC: from £80 | 
 
House EPC: from £85 | 
 
Legionella risk assessment: from £65 | 
 
EPC and legionella together: £120 | 

All prices plus VAT. Glasgow (G) and Edinburgh (EH) postcodes; £20 travel supplement elsewhere.

# Legionella Risk Assessment Edinburgh | From £65 | Scotland EPC
URL: https://scotlandepc.com/legionella-risk-assessment-edinburgh/

- Home
- Areas
- Legionella Edinburgh

## Legionella risk assessment Edinburgh

Legionella risk assessments for rented homes and short-term lets across Edinburgh. From £65 per property in EH postcodes, or £120 with an EPC, plus VAT.

### Short-term lets and HMOs

Edinburgh has a large number of short-term lets and HMOs. Short-term let hosts must meet the Repairing Standard, which includes the duty to assess legionella risk. Properties that sit empty between guests are a particular risk, because water stagnates in the pipes and shower hoses.

HMOs and larger flats often have shared tanks or long pipe runs. We will quote for these once we know the size of the system.

### Older tenements

New Town and Marchmont flats often have cylinders in cupboards and, on top floors, tanks in the roof space. Old pipework that once fed a removed bathroom or kitchen can leave dead legs, which the Repairing Standard guidance says should be removed.

### What we check

We identify the water system, measure temperatures at the taps, cylinder and any tank, inspect tanks for lids and debris, and look for showers, dead legs and little-used outlets. You get a written assessment with the temperatures recorded, an overall risk level and a short list of actions. More about legionella risk assessments.

Temperature bands from HSE guidance on legionella in hot and cold water systems.

### The rules in Scotland

The Repairing Standard guidance says a private landlord must have the water system assessed for legionella before the property is first let, and review it at intervals of no more than two years. There is no legionella certificate and water testing is not normally needed.

### Questions

Do short-term lets in Edinburgh need a legionella risk assessment?
Yes. Short-term lets must meet the Repairing Standard, which includes assessing legionella risk before letting and reviewing it at least every two years.
Can you do the EPC at the same time?
Yes. Both together cost £120 + VAT in EH postcodes.

## About Scotland EPC

Domestic EPCs and legionella risk assessments, done properly and priced clearly, from a Glasgow team that works in building energy every day.

### Who we are

Scotland EPC is the domestic service of Scottish Energy Services, an energy and building compliance consultancy based at 272 Bath Street in Glasgow city centre. Scottish Energy Services produces SAP and SBEM calculations, commercial EPCs and other compliance work for developers, architects and businesses. Scotland EPC brings the same standards to homes, landlords and letting agents.

### How we work

- Accredited assessors. Every EPC is produced by an accredited domestic energy assessor and lodged on the Scottish EPC Register.
 
- Clear prices. Starting prices by property type, plus VAT, confirmed before you book, with a single travel supplement outside G and EH postcodes.
 
- One visit for both. EPC and legionella risk assessment together, so your tenant or agent only gives access once.
 
- Quick paperwork. EPCs are normally lodged within 24 hours of the visit.
 
- Straight answers. If you have a question about your rating or the actions in a legionella assessment, call us.

SAP and SBEM calculations, commercial EPCs and building energy compliance for new builds, conversions and non-domestic buildings.

#### Fire Risk Scotland

Fire risk assessments for HMOs, short-term lets, workplaces, hotels, care homes and blocks of flats across Scotland.
